strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of generative retrieval: adaptation to heterogeneous retrieval tasks without task-specific relevance labels.
ZEROGR combines semantic document identifiers, instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, and constrained decoding in a coherent framework.
The evaluation covers many domains and includes comparisons with sparse, dense, instruction-tuned, and generative retrieval approaches.
The component studies examine document-identifier design, instruction-tuning diversity, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding behavior.
weaknesses: The headline claims are substantially stronger than the results. On MAIR, ZEROGR scores 41.1 Acc@1, below GTE-Qwen2-1.5B (44.4), E5-Mistral-7B (46.8), and GritLM-7B (47.0). On BEIR, its 48.1 nDCG@10 is also below several dense baselines, including BGE-Large (51.8), OpenAI Embed (54.2), and E5-Mistral (55.7). Thus the claimed state of the art and consistent superiority are unsupported.

The main MAIR average mixes seen and unseen tasks even though the paper is framed around zero-shot generalization. Moreover, the training collection includes MAIR and BEIR training tasks, including datasets also present in the reported evaluations. Results must be separated rigorously by task and dataset provenance to rule out benchmark leakage and task-family overlap.

The method constructs a new generative index by generating up to 16 queries per document and training a multi-billion-parameter retriever separately for every target corpus. No indexing time, GPU cost, memory use, latency, or scaling experiment with corpus size is reported. This makes the central claim of scalability unsubstantiated and leaves the comparison with inexpensive fixed dense indexes operationally unfair.

The learned natural-language identifiers can collide, but the paper does not explain how documents sharing an identifier are uniquely retrieved or ranked. A prefix-tree leaf represents an identifier rather than necessarily one document, creating an unresolved correctness issue in the document-level retrieval formulation.

Reverse-annealed decoding produces a stochastic list rather than a likelihood-ranked list, and its empirical advantage is extremely small. Figure 6 shows that it sacrifices Acc@1 relative to greedy decoding and offers only marginal changes in nDCG and recall, without repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analysis for its temperature parameters.

The evaluation has numerous internal inconsistencies: the setup says all 12 BEIR tasks, Table 2 reports 11, Figure 2 reports six, and the conclusion refers to seven; MAIR is variously described as 38, 69, or 126 tasks. These discrepancies make the experimental scope difficult to verify.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The retriever-training configuration, optimizer and schedule, batch sizes, number of pseudo-queries used in the main results, decoding parameters, per-corpus training cost, prompts for query generation, random seeds, and statistical variance are missing. The code/data footnote also contains no usable link.

Several comparisons are not clearly controlled for backbone, supervision, indexing budget, or corpus preprocessing. The generative baselines have results on only subsets of BEIR, while the dense baselines receive no analogous corpus-specific adaptation, limiting the strength of conclusions about the retrieval paradigm itself.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: adapting generative retrieval to heterogeneous tasks without labeled target-corpus queries.
The combination of natural-language document identifiers, instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, and constrained decoding is coherent and practically motivated.
The evaluation covers varied domains, and the paper includes useful component analyses of identifier design, task diversity, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding.
ZEROGR is competitive with several conventional retrievers and improves over the reported generative-retrieval baselines on multiple BEIR datasets.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art narrative is not supported by the aggregate results. On MAIR, ZEROGR scores 41.1 versus 46.8 for E5-Mistral and 47.0 for GritLM; on BEIR it scores 48.1 versus 55.7 for E5-Mistral and 54.2 for OpenAI Embed. The appendix also includes GTE-Qwen2-1.5B at 44.4 on MAIR, but this stronger baseline is omitted from the main comparison.

The zero-shot evaluation is compromised by substantial task overlap. ZeroGR-Train explicitly contains training data from many evaluated BEIR datasets, including SciFact, NFCorpus, SciDocs, FiQA, ArguAna, Quora, FEVER, and CQADupStack. The main MAIR average likewise mixes seen and unseen tasks, while separate subset averages are not reported.

Several performance claims are factually overstated. For example, ZEROGR is described as state of the art on Apple and MB, although it only ties the best result on Apple and is below BGE-Large on MB. Claims of consistently outperforming strong or instruction-tuned retrievers are similarly inconsistent with the tables.

The proposed identifier generator does not guarantee uniqueness, and Figure 4 confirms nonzero identifier-conflict rates. The paper never explains how multiple documents sharing an identifier are represented in the trie, ranked, or scored during evaluation, leaving a core part of the retrieval procedure technically ambiguous.

The claimed scalability is unsupported. ZEROGR generates numerous queries per document and fine-tunes a separate 3B-parameter model for every target corpus, yet reports no indexing time, GPU cost, memory footprint, corpus-size scaling, latency, or comparison with dense indexing. Referring only to the 3B retriever also ignores the additional 1B query and identifier generators.

The reverse-annealing results do not establish a clear advantage: greedy decoding matches its Acc@1, beam search slightly exceeds its nDCG@10, and nucleus sampling slightly exceeds its Recall@100. There are no significance tests, repeated runs, sensitivity analyses for the schedule parameters, or comparisons against simpler methods for interpolating precision and recall.

Comparisons with prior generative retrievers are incomplete and selective: results are missing on many BEIR datasets, no aggregate comparison is possible, and there are no generative baselines on MAIR. Consequently, the claim of establishing a new state of the art for instruction-driven generative retrieval is not convincingly demonstrated.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Important details such as the chosen number of pseudo-queries, reverse-annealing hyperparameters, batch sizes, training budgets, corpus preprocessing, collision handling, and evaluation sample sizes are missing. The manuscript states that code and data are available, but the corresponding footnote contains no link.

The manuscript is internally inconsistent about evaluation scope, variously claiming 12, 11, and seven BEIR datasets and 38 versus 69 MAIR tasks. No uncertainty estimates are provided despite highly variable task-level results.

The novelty is moderate: learned textual identifiers, synthetic-query indexing, instruction tuning, constrained decoding, and temperature scheduling are individually established ideas. The paper's main contribution is their integration, but the evaluation does not isolate instruction conditioning sufficiently or demonstrate that this integration overcomes the major limitations of dense retrieval.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and potentially important direction: extending generative retrieval to heterogeneous, instruction-specified tasks without task-specific relevance labels. The combination of learned semantic docids, instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, and constrained decoding forms a coherent framework.
The empirical study is broad, covering 38 MAIR tasks and 11 BEIR tasks across several domains, with comparisons to sparse, dense, instruction-tuned, and generative retrieval systems.

The ablations address several relevant design dimensions, including instruction-tuning diversity, docid representations, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding strategy. The learned docids substantially outperform the alternative identifiers in the controlled comparison.

Results on the genuinely unseen MAIR subset are encouraging: ZeroGR exceeds BM25 and OpenAI-Embed on average and is competitive with larger instruction-tuned dense retrievers despite using a 3B retrieval model.
The paper is generally well organized, and the method is easy to understand at a conceptual level.
weaknesses: Some headline claims are overstated. ZeroGR is not the overall best system in Table 2: its MAIR average of 41.1 is below GTE-Qwen2-1.5B, E5-Mistral-7B, and GritLM-7B, while its BEIR average of 48.1 trails several dense retrievers. The claimed state of the art therefore needs to be restricted specifically to an appropriately defined generative-retrieval setting.

The scalability claim is insufficiently supported. Adapting to every new corpus requires generating multiple queries per document and fine-tuning a 3B model as the corpus-specific index. The paper reports no indexing time, GPU requirements, query latency, model-storage cost, or experiments that scale corpus size, despite these being central practical concerns for generative retrieval.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper omits key hyperparameters for corpus-specific retriever training and reverse annealing, including batch size, training steps or epochs, learning-rate schedule, k, m, and maximum temperature. The default number of pseudo-queries and procedures for resolving duplicate docids are also unclear.

Generated docid collisions create an unresolved correctness issue because a shared identifier cannot uniquely retrieve multiple documents. Collision rates are measured but the paper does not explain how collisions are handled or quantify their effect, especially for large corpora.

The reverse-annealing evidence is limited to one aggregate ablation without uncertainty estimates. It ties greedy decoding on Acc@1, underperforms beam search on nDCG@10, and slightly underperforms nucleus sampling on recall, so the assertion that it offers the best balance would benefit from a defined combined objective, per-task results, and repeated-run variance.

The zero-shot evaluation presentation is confusing. The primary MAIR average mixes tasks seen during instruction tuning with unseen tasks, whereas the unseen subset is the evidence relevant to the central generalization claim. There are also inconsistencies in the reported evaluation scope: the setup mentions 12 BEIR tasks, Table 2 reports 11, and the conclusion refers to seven.

The comparison with prior generative retrievers is incomplete because many baseline entries are missing across BEIR tasks. This makes the broad claim of outperforming generative baselines difficult to establish uniformly. Statistical significance or confidence intervals are absent throughout.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of generative retrieval: adaptation to heterogeneous retrieval tasks without target-query supervision.
The framework is intuitive and combines instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, readable semantic document identifiers, and constrained decoding in a coherent pipeline.
Evaluation covers many tasks and domains across MAIR and BEIR, with useful analyses of document-identifier design, training-task diversity, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding strategy.
The proposed identifiers outperform several alternatives in the controlled ablation, and the query generator substantially improves the RQ-VAE baseline on average.
The authors appropriately acknowledge that the approach remains behind leading dense retrievers and has not been validated on million-document corpora.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot evidence is difficult to interpret. OpenInstIR includes training splits from several BEIR datasets later used for evaluation, while the primary MAIR average combines seen and unseen tasks. An aggregate result restricted to genuinely unseen tasks is not reported prominently. Consequently, the headline comparison does not cleanly establish task-level zero-shot generalization.

The paper claims scalability despite evaluating only moderately sized corpora. Every new corpus requires generating multiple queries per document and fine-tuning a 3B model; the reported 1.8-hour indexing time is only an estimate for 100K documents. There are no experiments at million-document scale, no scaling curves, and no measured end-to-end cost for top-100 retrieval.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The size and construction of the GPT-4o-generated document-identifier training set are unspecified, as are the main retriever's learning rate, epochs, batch size, default number of pseudo-queries, random seeds, reverse-annealing parameters, and substantial compute requirements. The advertised code link is also absent in the submitted manuscript.

The reverse-annealing evidence is weak. It does not outperform the alternatives on any reported metric: greedy matches its Acc@1, beam search slightly exceeds its nDCG@10, and nucleus sampling slightly exceeds its Recall@100. Because the method is stochastic, results also require repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and sensitivity analyses for its temperature parameters.

Comparisons with prior generative retrievers are incomplete and potentially confounded by different training data and modified inference procedures. Table 3 covers only six selected BEIR tasks, while Table 12 indicates that TIGER is retrained on OpenInstIR and decoded using the proposed reverse-annealing method. The paper does not clearly separate gains from training data, pseudo-query generation, document identifiers, and decoding in a full factorial comparison.

The empirical study provides no confidence intervals or significance tests despite small evaluation and ablation sets, often around 100 queries per task. Several improvements could therefore reflect sampling variability or benchmark/task weighting choices.

Dataset reporting is internally inconsistent: OpenInstIR is described as containing 69 tasks in Table 1, 60 tasks in Figure 2, and 66 tasks in the appendix, while the listed per-domain entries appear to imply yet another total. The manuscript also says BEIR has 12 tasks although the reported aggregate uses 11.

The technical novelty is primarily an integration of established ingredients—synthetic query indexing, natural-language identifiers, constrained decoding, and instruction tuning. Given the evaluation ambiguities and limited evidence for the new decoding component, the paper does not yet substantiate its broad claims of a generalizable and scalable zero-shot retrieval framework.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: adapting generative retrieval to heterogeneous retrieval tasks without task-specific relevance labels.
The proposed pipeline is coherent, combining semantic document identifiers, instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, and constrained decoding in a unified framework.
The evaluation covers heterogeneous domains, and the component analyses examine document-identifier design, query count, model size, training-task diversity, and decoding behavior.
ZEROGR substantially improves over several prior generative-retrieval results, while OpenInstIR could become a useful resource if fully documented and released.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot evidence is not sufficiently clean. OpenInstIR includes training splits from several BEIR and MAIR-related tasks, the main MAIR average mixes seen and unseen tasks, and no convincing document/query overlap or contamination audit is provided. Results on a clearly isolated unseen-task aggregate should be central.

The scalability claim is unsupported. Experiments explicitly focus on moderately sized corpora, with no evaluation near or above one million documents. The reported efficiency numbers are estimates for a single setting and do not clearly include the complete costs of identifier generation, pseudo-query generation, and per-corpus retriever training.

The method underperforms the strongest dense retrievers by substantial margins on MAIR and most modern dense baselines on BEIR. Its small advantage over OpenAI-Embed on MAIR is marginal, while E5-Mistral and GritLM are roughly six points better. Consequently, the broad competitiveness claims are overstated.

The contributions are individually incremental: synthetic document-to-query generation, natural-language or keyword identifiers, trie-constrained decoding, and temperature scheduling are established ideas. The paper does not demonstrate that their combination constitutes a sufficiently substantial technical advance.

The reverse-annealing evaluation is incomplete. Crucial parameters such as the maximum temperature are not fully specified, stochastic variability is not reported, and there are no repeated runs or significance tests. The comparison also does not establish superiority to score-based reranking or stronger diverse-decoding alternatives.

Generated identifiers still have a reported collision rate of 0.45%, but the paper does not explain how colliding documents are uniquely retrieved or ranked. The assertion that this does not meaningfully affect accuracy is not supported by a collision-aware analysis.

Reproducibility is weak: the code link is blank; retriever optimization details, prompts for query generation, data-mixture construction, sampling choices, random seeds, and several decoding settings are missing. OpenInstIR is inconsistently described as containing 60, 66, or 69 tasks, and licensing and release details are absent.

The ablations do not isolate instruction conditioning convincingly. There is no direct comparison between otherwise identical generators with and without task instructions, and the paper is inconsistent about whether the document-identifier generator is conditioned on instructions.

Several experimental inconsistencies reduce confidence: the text and tables disagree about the number of BEIR tasks, prior generative baselines are compared using different training data or only partial dataset coverage, and the new dataset's split construction is insufficiently documented.

OpenInstIR aggregates medical, legal, code, and social-media data, and uses a proprietary model for identifier supervision, but the paper provides no meaningful discussion of licensing, privacy, harmful-content filtering, dataset bias, or the reproducibility implications of proprietary-model-generated labels.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: extending generative retrieval to heterogeneous, instruction-specified retrieval tasks without target relevance labels.

ZEROGR is a coherent framework combining semantic document identifiers, instruction-conditioned pseudo-query generation, and constrained reverse-annealed decoding. The components are intuitive and practically motivated.

The evaluation spans many domains and includes strong sparse, dense, instruction-tuned, and generative baselines. On MAIR, the 3B model is competitive with OpenAI embeddings and substantially improves over several conventional retrievers; it also advances over prior generative retrieval methods on the reported BEIR tasks.

The ablations cover several relevant design choices, including identifier type, instruction-tuning diversity, pseudo-query count, model size, and decoding. The semantic identifier ablation shows a meaningful gain over RQ-VAE and other alternatives.

OpenInstIR could be a valuable community resource because it aggregates diverse retrieval tasks, relevance annotations, and instructions across academic, code, finance, legal, medical, and web domains.
The paper is generally well organized, and it appropriately acknowledges the substantial indexing cost and lack of experiments on million-document corpora.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot evaluation is not sufficiently clean. OpenInstIR includes training splits from MAIR and BEIR tasks such as SciFact, NFCorpus, FiQA, and ArguAna. The headline MAIR average mixes seen and unseen tasks, while BEIR results are presented as zero-shot despite target-task training data being used for the generators. Separate aggregate results for strictly unseen tasks should be central rather than only per-task appendix entries.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits the size and construction details of the GPT-4o-generated document-identifier data, the default pseudo-query count, generative-retriever optimization hyperparameters, prompt templates for query generation and retrieval, reverse-annealing values for Tmax/k/m, random seeds, and hardware or training-time details. The abstract also states that code is available but provides no URL.

The OpenInstIR statistics are internally inconsistent: the paper variously reports 69 tasks, 66 tasks, and 60 tasks, while the datasets listed in Table 4 appear to total yet another number. This weakens confidence in the dataset contribution and experimental accounting.

The reported evaluation uses small query samples—roughly 100 or fewer queries for many tasks—and provides neither confidence intervals nor significance tests. This is especially problematic for stochastic reverse-annealed decoding, for which results may depend on sampling seeds.

The novelty of the individual components is moderate. Semantic/title-like identifiers, pseudo-query indexing, instruction tuning, and sampling-based constrained decoding all closely build on existing ideas; reverse annealing is a relatively simple heuristic and is not theoretically justified.

The reverse-annealing evidence is limited to six small development tasks. It is not the best method on every metric, sensitivity to its schedule is absent, and comparisons do not report repeated stochastic runs or latency for retrieving 100 documents.

Scalability remains a major unresolved issue. Each new corpus requires generating many pseudo-queries and fine-tuning a retriever, yet experiments focus on moderately sized corpora. The efficiency table reports estimates for only a 100K-document setting and top-1 retrieval, rather than measured end-to-end costs at realistic corpus sizes and top-100 decoding.

Some comparisons with prior generative retrieval systems are difficult to interpret because coverage differs across methods and adapted baselines use OpenInstIR and the proposed decoding procedure. A controlled comparison isolating training data, identifier design, and decoding is needed.

Overall, the approach is promising and the results are encouraging, but the target-task overlap, mixed seen/unseen headline evaluation, incomplete reproducibility information, and limited scalability evidence leave the main generalization claims slightly below the acceptance threshold.
